title: Relay Studio Help
introduction: Search this offline guide for the task you are trying to complete. Relay Studio keeps projects, requests, flows, saved responses, and diagnostics on your computer and does not require a hosted workspace.

sections.title: Getting Started
sections.body: A Relay Studio workspace combines a local project, an active environment, reusable REST requests, multi-step flows, and saved response evidence.
steps: Create a project or open a local .restproj file from File or the command palette.
Choose the active environment and set baseUrl before sending a request.
Create requests manually or import selected operations from an OpenAPI definition.
Save the project before closing Relay Studio so request and flow changes remain available.

sections.title: Projects And Saving
sections.body: Projects are local .restproj files containing requests, flows, environments, variables, saved-response metadata, import history, and workspace settings.
steps: Use Save Project As the first time you choose a project location.
Use Save Project or Cmd+S on macOS and Ctrl+S on Windows and Linux for later changes.
A dot on a request or flow tab indicates unsaved work.
Do not edit the same project concurrently in multiple Relay Studio windows. Concurrent native saves are rejected rather than silently overwriting changes.

sections.title: Environments, Variables, And Credentials
sections.body: Environment variables provide reusable values such as baseUrl and runtime authentication values. Reference a variable with double braces, for example {{accountId}}.
steps: Open the Inspector and edit variables for the active environment.
Mark credential values secret and use variable names in Bearer, Basic, API-key, OAuth, or custom-header authorization settings.
Use a path template such as /api/accounts/{accountId}, then set the accountId path parameter value to {{accountId}} so the value is URL-encoded.
Never paste production passwords, tokens, cookies, or private keys into an imported definition, generated example, saved response, or issue report.

sections.title: Requests
sections.body: Relay Studio supports GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, and OPTIONS requests with headers, query parameters, path parameters, authentication, retry, timeout, and cancellation controls.
steps: Select a request in Explorer and review its method, path, active environment, authorization, parameters, headers, and body.
Choose Send Request and inspect status, headers, final URL, timing, formatted body, and Console events.
Select Cancel Request to stop an in-progress request.
In a formatted JSON response, select a same-origin HTTP(S) URL to create a new GET request with an independent copy of the source authorization profile.

sections.title: JSON, Form, And Multipart Bodies
sections.body: Request bodies can be JSON, plain text, URL-encoded form data, or multipart form data.
steps: For JSON, enter valid JSON and use Format or Minify when reviewing it.
For URL-encoded forms, add enabled name/value fields; Relay Studio creates the Content-Type header.
For multipart forms, choose text or file for each field. File access requires explicit approval for the current session and destination origin.
Relay Studio does not persist active local file authority in the project. Reapprove multipart files after reopening the project or changing the destination origin.

sections.title: OpenAPI Import And Saving
sections.body: Import selected Swagger 2.0 or OpenAPI 3.x operations from a direct JSON/YAML URL or a Swagger UI page while keeping operation selection explicit.
steps: Open File > Import API Definition or run Import API Docs from the command palette.
Enter the Swagger UI or direct definition URL. Review and approve any secondary definition destination before Relay Studio retrieves it.
Review the discovered operations and select only the requests you want.
Choose Add N Selected to add requests without saving yet, or Add and Save N Selected to add them and open the Save Project dialog.
Review imported base URLs, authentication placeholders, examples, form fields, multipart fields, external references, and deprecated operations before sending anything.
Relay Studio never imports example credentials as usable secrets. Supply approved local values separately.

sections.title: Flows And Response Mappings
sections.body: Flows run requests in dependency order. Success and failure paths determine which later steps run, and response mappings capture JSON values as temporary variables.
steps: Create or open a flow, add request steps, and connect each success or failure path.
Select a source step, open Response Mappings > Manage, and choose Add Mapping.
Enter a variable name and a supported JSONPath such as $.accessToken, $.user.id, or $.items[0].id.
Mark authentication mappings secret. Credential-shaped paths and variable names are treated as secret even when the checkbox is cleared.
Use the mapped variable in a later request header, query value, body field, or path-parameter value with {{variableName}}.
Captured values exist only during that flow run and are not written back into the saved project environment.

sections.title: Flows: Use The First List Result
sections.body: Use an indexed JSONPath mapping when one request returns a named array and the next request needs a key from its first row.
steps: Connect Login success to Parts List, then connect Parts List success to Get Part.
On Login, map $.accessToken into the secret variable accessToken and configure both part requests to use that Bearer variable.
If the list response is {"items":[{"partNumber":"IMP-CSV-1001"}]}, map $.items[0].partNumber into firstPartKey on the Parts List step.
Configure Get Part with the path /api/config/parts/{partKey} and an enabled path parameter named partKey whose value is {{firstPartKey}}.
Run the flow and inspect Console events to confirm accessToken and firstPartKey were captured before Get Part ran.

If the API returns a top-level array, root-array syntax such as $[0].partNumber is not currently supported. Use a response with a named array property or capture a deterministic identifier another way.

sections.title: Running And Debugging Flows
sections.body: Flow results show each step as success, failed, skipped, or blocked and retain runtime variables only for the current execution.
steps: Choose Run Flow and inspect node status plus the Console utility tab.
A failed response mapping identifies its source step, JSONPath, and destination variable. Success-dependent steps are skipped afterward.
An empty list, missing field, malformed JSON response, unsupported JSONPath, or missing request dependency stops the affected path actionably.
Use Cancel Flow to stop the active request and prevent remaining steps from starting.
For reliable first-row workflows, make sure the API defines a deterministic sort order; otherwise the first item can change between runs.

sections.title: Saved Responses And Comparison
sections.body: Save redacted response artifacts as local evidence, reopen them from Explorer, and compare two saved responses while debugging API changes.
steps: After a request or flow response, choose Save Response and select a JSON or text destination.
Confirm explicitly before overwriting an existing artifact.
In Explorer, select exactly two saved responses for comparison and choose Compare selected responses.
Review status, header, timing, text, or JSON-path differences in the Response dock.
Inspect every artifact before sharing it even though Relay Studio applies shared credential redaction.

sections.title: Code Examples
sections.body: Generate local, read-only HTTP, cURL, C#, Java, jQuery, Node.js, PHP, Python, or Ruby examples from an open request or flow without executing it.
steps: Right-click a request or flow tab, choose Generate Code, then choose a language.
Review credential and multipart-file placeholders, switch languages if needed, and choose Copy Code.
Replace <REDACTED> and other credential masks securely at runtime; generated examples never reveal stored credential values.
For flows, implement the displayed branch prerequisites. Java and jQuery examples capture and reuse supported scalar response mappings automatically.
Java response mapping requires Jackson Databind and rejects non-success, empty, malformed, missing, null, or non-scalar mapping responses actionably.

sections.title: Recovery And Backups
sections.body: Relay Studio validates project schema, uses atomic native saves, and keeps a recovery backup for the last valid project state.
steps: Follow the displayed recovery guidance when a project is invalid or incomplete.
Restore the backup only when the primary project cannot be opened.
Legacy projects receive typed defaults where migration is supported; malformed nested project state is rejected instead of guessed.
Keep a separate copy before manually editing a .restproj file.

sections.title: Diagnostics And Security
sections.body: Diagnostics export includes application, platform, project counts, and recent Console context with known secrets redacted.
steps: Export diagnostics from Settings > Workspace.
Inspect the generated JSON before sharing it.
Relay Studio keeps project persistence local and does not upload workspace data to a hosted Relay Studio service.
Never include passwords, bearer tokens, cookies, API keys, private keys, or private project data in issue reports.

sections.title: Troubleshooting Requests And Imports
sections.body: Start with the visible error and Console events; Relay Studio reports validation, HTTP, timeout, cancellation, mapping, import, persistence, and security failures separately.
steps: For an Invalid or non-JSON response, verify the endpoint, HTTP status, credentials, Content-Type, and response body before applying a JSON mapping.
For 401 or 403, verify the selected environment and authentication variable without pasting its value into diagnostics.
For an unresolved variable, confirm its spelling, active environment, or preceding flow mapping and success path.
For an import failure, verify the direct definition URL or review the secondary Swagger UI destination, external reference origin, circular reference, and response size.
For native/browser differences, test in the packaged desktop app when file access, proxy behavior, redirects, or operating-system persistence is involved.

sections.title: Keyboard And Navigation
sections.body: Native menus and the command palette expose the primary workspace actions without requiring pointer navigation.
steps: Open command search with Cmd+K on macOS or Ctrl+K on Windows and Linux.
Save with Cmd+S or Ctrl+S and send or run with Cmd+Enter or Ctrl+Enter.
Use the View menu to toggle Explorer, Inspector, Response Dock, and Flow Details.
Press Escape to dismiss command palettes, dialogs, and context menus without taking an action.
